newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: FOCUS-Tajik aluminium output stable despite clashes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tajik aluminium output stable despite clashes.

text.p: Tursunzade aluminium smelter, Tajikistan's main hard currency earner, is working without interruption despite recent armed clashes in the area, a senior plant official said.
"The plant's work has not been interrupted despite the recent clashes between local gangs and pro-government forces," plant director Abdukadyr Ermatov told Reuters in an interview.

The plant produced 198,000 tonnes of aluminium in 1996, down on 1995's 237,500 tonnes and just 40 percent of annual capacity of 500,000 tonnes. Ermatov said he was hopeful output this year could be sustained at last year's levels.

Earlier this month, Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, the mutinous commander of Tajikistan's elite armoured brigade, stormed the town where the smelter is based to unseat local strongman Kodir Abdulayev.

Since January last year the town, 45 km west of the capital Dushanbe, has been the scene of frequent bloody clashes among local gang leaders for control over the plant, the former Soviet republic's only stable dollar earner besides narcotics and a declining cotton crop.
Ermatov said "no military groups tried to sneak on to the territory of the smelter during the recent fighting".
"But the clashes near the plant have shocked many of our workers, who had to come to work amidst shooting...The delivery of alumina, bought mostly from Ukraine, has also fallen."
Ermatov said the plant had been severely hit by a sharp rise, more than two-fold, in transport tariffs last year.

"But the present-day situation on international metals markets is very favourable for us. Aluminium prices have gone up to some $1,600 per tonne from around $1,200 last year," he said. "It can somehow recompense for huge transportation costs."

But the smelter, guarded by 60 security ministry servicemen, is still in the epicentre of gangster warfare, and it is unclear if criminal warlords will obey President Imomali Rakhmonov's call at the weekend to lay down guns.
"As long as persons with Kalashnikov guns roam around, one can't talk of real order and stability of output," Ermatov said.
The plant also owes a total of $120 million for foreign credits granted in previous years.
But Ermatov hoped the situation would change drastically this year.

"The smelter, now state-owned, has been included in the privatisation programmme for 1997...Most probably, its control share will remain in state hands, but the remaining part could be sold to foreign investors," he said.

The cash-strapped management has already started reducing the number of personnel. The smelter now provides jobs for 13,000 workers but operates at only 40 percent of its capacity. In the past three months 800 workers have lost their jobs.
